blocks.text: 1. Sliding Window Chunking

blocks.alt: A document goes through a sliding window to produce overlapping chunks

blocks.text: Sliding Window Chunking covers how overlapping windows can preserve context across chunk boundaries, tackling the boundary problem from a different angle.
It lets consecutive chunks share a portion of their content instead of cutting cleanly.
2. The Hard Boundary Problem
As covered under broken meaning at boundaries in Fixed Chunking, even a well chosen cut point still separates two chunks completely, with zero shared content.
Information right at that boundary can lose context on both sides.
3. What A Window Is

blocks.alt: A window size defines a fixed span of text

blocks.text: A window is a fixed size span of text that slides forward by less than its own length.
Each step forward reuses part of the previous window's content.
4. Step Size Versus Window Size

blocks.alt: Step size decides how far to move while window size decides how much to include

blocks.text: The window size sets how much text each chunk holds; the step size sets how far it moves forward.
A smaller step relative to the window creates more overlap between neighbors.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Parameter","What it controls"],"rows":[["Window size","How much text each chunk holds"],["Step size","How far the window moves forward, and thus overlap amount"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Overlap Regions In Practice

blocks.alt: Chunk 1 and chunk 2 share an overlap region

blocks.text: The overlap region appears at the end of one chunk and again at the start of the next.
That shared text gives both neighboring chunks a bit of surrounding context.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A sentence that would have been split cleanly in half under fixed chunking often appears complete in at least one of the two overlapping chunks under sliding window chunking.

blocks.text: 6. Cost Of Overlap

blocks.alt: More overlap means more storage and compute

blocks.text: Overlapping content gets stored and embedded more than once.
This trades extra storage and compute for better boundary context.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A high overlap ratio can inflate the total number of stored chunks substantially. Doubling the overlap on a large collection means storing and embedding a meaningfully larger volume of text overall.

blocks.text: 7. Sliding Window Versus Recursive

blocks.alt: Sliding window uses fixed overlap while recursive is structure-aware

blocks.text: Recursive Chunking chooses smarter cut points; sliding windows instead soften the cut itself.
These are two different, complementary answers to the same boundary problem.
8. Combining With Other Strategies
A sliding window can be layered on top of recursive or fixed chunking.
These strategies are not mutually exclusive alternatives, but combinable techniques.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Base strategy","With overlap added"],"rows":[["Fixed chunking","Fixed sized chunks that share boundary text"],["Recursive chunking","Structurally aware chunks that also share boundary text"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Sliding Window Chunking Is Worth The Overlap Cost

blocks.alt: Needing continuity across chunk boundaries points toward sliding window chunking

blocks.text: Content where cross boundary continuity matters most benefits from sliding windows.
Storage constrained collections, by contrast, may prefer to avoid the extra overlap cost.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates building overlapping chunks with a sliding window.

code.content:
document = (
    "Machine learning models learn patterns from data. "
    "Training requires large datasets and significant compute. "
    "Once trained, models can make predictions on new inputs. "
    "Evaluation measures how well those predictions generalize."
)

def sliding_window_chunk(text, window_size, step_size):
    # slide a fixed size window forward by less than its own length
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        chunk = text[start:start + window_size]
        chunks.append(chunk)
        start += step_size  # smaller steps relative to window size create more overlap
    return chunks

chunks = sliding_window_chunk(document, window_size=80, step_size=50)

print(f"Overlap per step: {80 - 50} characters\n")
for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
    print(f"  Chunk {i}: {chunk!r}")

print("\nNotice the tail of each chunk reappears at the start of the next,")
print("preserving context across the boundary.")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the last thirty characters of each chunk reappearing as the first thirty characters of the next, preserving context that a clean cut would have discarded.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Setting the step size equal to the window size, which produces no overlap at all.
Choosing an overlap ratio so high that storage and embedding costs balloon unnecessarily.
Assuming sliding windows alone fix boundary problems without ever combining them with recursive chunking.
Forgetting that overlapping chunks can surface as near duplicate results in retrieval if overlap is excessive.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Sliding window chunking lets consecutive chunks share a portion of their content instead of cutting cleanly.
A clean cut point still separates two chunks completely, with zero shared content, unless overlap is added.
A window is a fixed size span of text that slides forward by less than its own length.
Window size controls chunk content; step size controls how far the window moves, and thus overlap amount.
The overlap region appears at the end of one chunk and again at the start of the next.
Overlapping content costs extra storage and compute, since it gets stored and embedded more than once.
Sliding windows soften cuts; recursive chunking chooses smarter cuts, two complementary approaches.
A sliding window can be layered on top of fixed or recursive chunking rather than replacing them.
